But we don't know exactly. Let's assume it returns a dict with t_statistic, p_value, df, reject_null, and maybe confidence_interval. We'll produce a reasonable interpretation.

We should compute manually? Let's quickly approximate: sample1: [22,33,42,12,34] mean = (22+33+42+12+34)=143/5=28.6. sample2: [23,45,44,14,38] sum=164/5=32.8. Compute standard deviations: sample1 variance: sum((x-mean)^2): (22-28.6)^2=43.56, (33-28.6)^2=19.36, (42-28.6)^2=176.36, (12-28.6)^2=273.16, (34-28.6)^2=29.16. Sum=~581.6. Sample variance s1^2=581.6/(n1-1)=581.6/4=145.4. s1=12.07. Sample2: differences: (23-32.8)^2=96.04, (45-32.8)^2=148.84, (44-32.8)^2=125.44, (14-32.8)^2=352.84, (38-32.8)^2=27.04. Sum=~650.2. s2^2=650.2/4=162.55. s2=12.75. Pooled variance? For equal variances assumption: sp^2 = ((n1-1)s1^2 + (n2-1)s2^2)/(n1+n2-2) = (4*145.4 + 4*162.55)/8 = (581.6+650.2)/8=1231.8/8=153.975. sp=12.41. Standard error of difference: sqrt(sp^2*(1/n1+1/n2))=sqrt(153.975*(0.4))=sqrt(61.59)=7.85. t = (28.6-32.8)/7.85 = -4.2/7.85=-0.535. df=8. p-value two-sided ~0.6. So fail to reject null. So conclusion: no significant difference.

But the function might use Welch's t-test by default. That would give slightly different t. Let's compute Welch: se = sqrt(s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2) = sqrt(145.4/5 + 162.55/5) = sqrt(29.08+32.51)=sqrt(61.59)=7.85 same as above because n equal. df = (s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2)^2 / ((s1^2/n1)^2/(n1-1)+(s2^2/n2)^2/(n2-1)). Compute numerator: 61.59^2=3793.9. Denominator: (29.08^2/4)+(32.51^2/4)= (846.5/4)+(1057.5/4)=211.6+264.4=476.0. df=3793.9/476=7.97 ~8. So same. So t ~ -0.535, p ~0.6. So we interpret.
